comments.text: Voxtral 3 is Mistral’s new family of speech models: speech-to-text, text-to-speech and a voice agent SDK, all through Mistral’s API.Problem: Building a voice agent usually means gluing together separate pieces for transcription, reasoning and speech. Transcription also tends to break down on real calls, with several speakers, domain terms and many languages, and robotic voices make conversations feel stiff.Solution: Voxtral 3 covers the full loop. There are batch and realtime transcription models, a text-to-speech model, and an SDK built on LiveKit that combines listening, reasoning, tool calling and speaking in one real-time pipeline.What makes it different: Each stage of the voice agent is a separate model, so you can swap the LLM, the voice or the language. Transcription handles context biasing with keyterms or free-form text, no fine-tuning needed, and the TTS adapts emotion, pacing and emphasis to the conversation. Per Mistral, realtime transcription runs under 500 ms, and a full agent turn completes in under a second.Key features:Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 for the highest accuracy, with speaker diarization and context biasingVoxtral Mini Transcribe 3 for batch transcription (4B parameters)Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime 3 for agents, with sub-500 ms latencyVoxtral Mini TTS 3 with emotion, pacing and emphasis controls, and voice cloning from about 30 minutes of audioTranscription in 50+ languages, and TTS in 35+ languages and 50+ dialectsVoice agent SDK with function calling, web search, SIP telephony and WebRTCSelf-deployment and on-prem through Mistral salesPricing per Mistral: batch transcription from $0.0035 per minute, realtime transcription at $0.008 per minute, TTS at $13 per 1M characters, and the voice agent API from $0.04 per minute.Who it’s for: Developers and teams building voice agents, call transcription, or multilingual voice apps who want one provider for the whole pipeline.

Hi Product Hunt,I'm Arick, co-founder and CEO of BAND. Today we're launching BAND for Developers.If you run more than one coding agent, you know the pattern. Each agent is fast on its own, but they can't talk to each other, so you become the go-between. You copy context from one session into the next, tell the test agent what the refactor agent just changed, and find out an hour later that two agents made opposite assumptions about the same interface. More agents should mean more work done. Instead, a lot of it turns into more coordination for you.Most multi-agent dev tools today give you a better dispatch board. You assign tasks, agents run in parallel, you review what comes back. That helps with throughput, but every handoff still goes through a human.BAND for Developers lets the agents work it out between themselves:- Connect the agents you already run. Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot and OpenCode agents join shared rooms across machines. You keep your IDE, your terminal and your workflow.- Agents collaborate directly. They message each other, delegate, review each other's work and unblock one another. They can pull in a teammate's agent when the work needs it. Plans, decisions and work state live in the room rather than inside one session, so they survive when a session ends.- You step in when it matters. You keep working from the terminal. BAND desktop shows what's moving, what's blocked and which agent is waiting on you. Open the room, answer the question or redirect the agent, then step back out while the rest of the work keeps going.The difference is that the agents aren't only running side by side. comments.text: Hi Product Hunt, I'm Asaph, Head of Product at Flagsmith. Product and Engineering teams have been using Flagsmith flags for years to release safely. Plenty of them already split traffic with our multivariate flags, and then try to track and join exposure and conversion events using other tools to see whether the change worked. Many teams stop before getting any results, or find the process so complicated that they never try again. So we built the other half into Flagsmith - Today we’re launching Flagsmith Experiments as a public beta, in the open-source core and on Flagsmith Cloud. How it works: - Start from an A/B flag you already run, in your code, using our SDKs - Connect your warehouse - we currently support ClickHouse and Databricks, and BigQuery and Snowflake will be available soon. On our Flagsmith Cloud you can use a fully managed warehouse with a 2-click setup. - Create an Experiment with a hypothesis, and pick the audience using Flagsmith Segments or from external cohorts we sync with (we support Amplitude and Mixpanel) - Create a metric from your events, or use an existing one from your warehouse. - Get results based on a Bayesian engine, with Chance to beat and Lift indicators. - End the experiment and you're back on the flag - roll out the winner or roll back Where the data lives is your call. Bring-your-own-warehouse is part of the open-source edition. We kept v1 small on purpose: a Bayesian engine, one primary metric per experiment, and SDKs for JavaScript, React, Python, Java, Node.js, Go and Flutter. The fastest way to get started is to use our prebuilt prompt with your favorite coding agent, visit our docs for more info. One thing that surprised us while dogfooding this ourselves is that our experiments gave us better questions more often than final answers. That’s why we designed it to show the result, and a possible recommendation, but the call is still yours. What would you need to run your next experiment here? Gagan, Wadii, both Matts and I are here to discuss and answer your questions (while we’re actually together at our engineering offsite in Portugal!). And to help you get started we’re offering the first 20 teams a free 30-min setup session with me - to claim your session let me know in the comments what you’d test first!

comments.text: We're launching the general availability of Jockey today, and it's shaped by what we learned during the research preview. We heard three things loud and clear:People needed the connectors to work better. The strongest reactions came through Claude and ChatGPT. So we prioritized ChatGPT support for GA and made the MCP experience seamless. If you want to query your library, your chat interface should be the last friction point, not the first.Builders needed output they could control. Developers told us a black-box "final edit" wasn't what they wanted. They needed structured clips, JSON, artifacts they could manipulate. So we built durable artifacts that can be saved, shared, revoked, or deleted and ensured the API gives you timestamped, actionable output you own, not a render you're stuck with.Users wanted deep social intelligence, not just basic video search. Creators and marketers kept asking us: "Why is this video trending? What specific hooks are holding attention? What common patterns make these reels go viral?" We listened, and built social intelligence features that analyze video hooks, breakdown visual and audio pacing, and explain what actually works across trending content. We also added social ingestion of URL links from YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram Reels, so users can analyze what's working in the wild and search performance alongside content without having to upload videos. It's a whole new way to deconstruct viral video performance.Library-level understanding is the point. You point Jockey at thousands of videos and images, and it reasons across all of them, not just one. That's why we built it this way, and why every model upgrade makes it better without you lifting a finger.If you're building a video app, organizing footage, or trying to find something in thousands of hours of content, Jockey is for you. Hi Product Hunt,I'm Arick, co-founder and CEO of BAND. Today we're launching BAND for Developers.If you run more than one coding agent, you know the pattern. Each agent is fast on its own, but they can't talk to each other, so you become the go-between. You copy context from one session into the next, tell the test agent what the refactor agent just changed, and find out an hour later that two agents made opposite assumptions about the same interface. More agents should mean more work done. Instead, a lot of it turns into more coordination for you.Most multi-agent dev tools today give you a better dispatch board. You assign tasks, agents run in parallel, you review what comes back. That helps with throughput, but every handoff still goes through a human.BAND for Developers lets the agents work it out between themselves:- Connect the agents you already run. Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot and OpenCode agents join shared rooms across machines. You keep your IDE, your terminal and your workflow.- Agents collaborate directly. They message each other, delegate, review each other's work and unblock one another. They can pull in a teammate's agent when the work needs it. Plans, decisions and work state live in the room rather than inside one session, so they survive when a session ends.- You step in when it matters. You keep working from the terminal. BAND desktop shows what's moving, what's blocked and which agent is waiting on you. Open the room, answer the question or redirect the agent, then step back out while the rest of the work keeps going.The difference is that the agents aren't only running side by side. They coordinate while the work is happening, so many of the handoffs you'd normally do yourself happen without you. And you don't have to move your whole team onto one vendor's agents to get there.BAND desktop is free. Download it at band.ai/use-cases/band-desktop. comments.text: Hi Product Hunt, I'm William! I made Rill because I want to always stay in the flow. As an ADHD, I never liked code-switching. My best ideas for work come when I'm supposedly not working at all: watching something for fun, reading things and following a rabbit hole, looking at how someone else solved a problem. Then when an idea hit me, I'd have to stop, switch to coding agents, find the project and explain it all, and most of the time I just didn't.Rill is my way of removing that code-switching. It's a browser with your Claude Code or Codex working alongside you. When something on a page gives you an idea, you say so right there, and an agent starts on it in the right project. Full disclosure — I'm a big fan of Anthropic and actually built an app that works exclusively with Claude Desktop for secure local file search. So I've spent a lot of time thinking about this space.My concern with Cowork isn't the vision, it's the architecture. Agentic tasks burn through tokens fast (Anthropic says so themselves), so that $200/month cap can disappear quicker than you'd expect. And at that price, you'd want to use it for real work — but the whole thing requires giving Claude direct read/write/delete access to your files. If you're handling client data, patient records, or anything regulated, you're basically out.The bigger issue is prompt injection. Anthropic admits "the chances of an attack are still non-zero" — and back in October 2025, researchers showed exactly that: a prompt injection against Claude that pulled up to 30MB of user data per request through Anthropic's own API. When you're talking about an agent with file system access, email connectors, and a browser, that's not some theoretical edge case.There's a reason some of us build tools where Claude can search your files without actually touching them. The agentic future is definitely coming, but "AI that can access everything" and "AI that keeps you in control" are two very different products for two very different users.
